title: De la loi du contraste simultané des couleurs et de l'assortiment des objets colorés
edition: English translation by Charles Martel, The Principles of Harmony and Contrast of Colours, 1854
authority: Chevreul was director of dyes at the Gobelins tapestry works and a leading chemist; the book is the founding systematic account of simultaneous contrast and shaped Impressionist and Neo-Impressionist practice.
caveats: Observational and qualitative; explanations are pre-physiological and some rules of harmony are taste, not data. Phenomena themselves are real and well replicated.

title: An opponent-process theory of color vision
authority: Hurvich and Jameson quantified Ewald Hering's 1878 opponent-colors idea with hue-cancellation psychophysics; the paper is the canonical statement of opponent-process theory.
caveats: Cone-opponent axes found physiologically in the LGN (Derrington, Krauskopf and Lennie 1984) do not coincide exactly with the perceptual unique-hue axes, so a further cortical stage is needed. Unique hue loci vary between observers.

title: A Color Notation
edition: Later editions published by Munsell Color Company; Munsell Book of Color from 1929
authority: Munsell was a painter and art teacher who built the first widely used system ordering color by perceived equal steps of hue, value and chroma; it became the basis of US soil, geology and later colorimetric standards.
caveats: The original 1905 spacing was visually imperfect; the 1943 Munsell Renotation (Newhall, Nickerson, Judd, JOSA 33) corrected it. The color solid is irregular, not a regular sphere.

title: Interaction of Color
authority: Albers taught at the Bauhaus, Black Mountain College and Yale; the book is the most influential experiential course in color relativity for designers.
caveats: Pedagogy by exercise, with no controlled data and no quantified claims. The phenomena it demonstrates (induction, assimilation, vibration, transparency) are established in vision science.

title: Basic Color Terms: Their Universality and Evolution
authority: Berlin and Kay were Berkeley anthropologists/linguists; the book launched modern cross-language color naming research.
caveats: Evolutionary stage sequence is contested (Lucy, Roberson and Davies on Berinmo and Himba; Saunders and van Brakel). The World Color Survey (Kay, Berlin, Maffi, Merrifield and Cook 2009) supports partial universals with weaker strict stages.

title: Color Appearance Models
authority: Fairchild directs the Munsell Color Science Laboratory at RIT; the standard graduate text linking CIE colorimetry, appearance phenomena and models such as CIECAM02.
caveats: Models fit viewing conditions of controlled experiments; displays with unusual surrounds, HDR and small-field UI elements are less well covered. The 3rd ed. predates CAM16 (Li et al. 2017) and Oklab.

title: Visual sensitivities to color differences in daylight
container: Journal of the Optical Society of America
authority: MacAdam was a leading Kodak/Eastman and later Rochester color scientist; this paper measured the chromaticity discrimination ellipses that justified every later uniform color space.
caveats: Measured on essentially one observer (PGN) at one luminance and field size; later data (Brown and MacAdam 1949, Wyszecki and Fielder 1971) show larger ellipses and observer variation.

title: Color use guidelines for mapping and visualization
authority: Brewer (Penn State cartographer) created the ColorBrewer schemes; this chapter defines qualitative, sequential and diverging scheme typology.
caveats: Scoped to choropleth (area) maps; guidance on small marks and thin lines needs adaptation. Page range reported variously (123-147 or 123-148). Companion: Harrower and Brewer 2003, The Cartographic Journal 40(1), 27-37, on ColorBrewer.

title: Data visualization: the end of the rainbow
authority: IBM Research perceptual scientists who built rule-based colormap selection (PRAVDA) and argued against default rainbow maps.
caveats: Trade-magazine article rather than a controlled experiment; claims are backed by the authors' earlier perceptual work. Rainbow maps are not universally bad (Ware, Stone and Szafir 2023).

title: Rainbow color map (still) considered harmful
authority: Visualization researchers at UNC Chapel Hill; the paper is the most cited short critique of rainbow colormaps.
caveats: Opinion and example based, not a new experiment. Counter-argument: Ware, Stone and Szafir 2023, Rainbow colormaps are not all bad, IEEE CG&A, argue rainbows aid some tasks (high-resolution value reading).

title: Color sequences for univariate maps: theory, experiments and principles
authority: Colin Ware (UNH Data Visualization Research Lab) is a leading authority on perception for visualization.
caveats: Small experiments by modern standards; the form hypothesis was only partly supported. Findings were later folded into Ware's Information Visualization (2000, 4th ed. 2020).

title: A perceptual color space for image processing
authority: Ottosson is a graphics engineer; Oklab was adopted into CSS Color Module Levels 4 and 5 (W3C) and by major browsers and design tools, which gives it standards-body standing.
caveats: Self-published, not peer reviewed; fitted to CAM16 and IPT data rather than new experiments. Not perfectly uniform in lightness or hue everywhere (blues, very dark colors).

title: Aesthetic response to color combinations: preference, harmony, and similarity
authority: Palmer (UC Berkeley) and Schloss (Wisconsin) are leading experimental color-aesthetics researchers; this is the most careful modern test of harmony claims.
caveats: Western undergraduate samples, pairs of flat patches on a neutral ground; does not test real interfaces. Findings are averages; individuals vary widely (individual preference-harmony correlations ranged from about -.03 to +.70).

title: A colour harmony model for two-colour combinations
authority: Luo (Leeds, Zhejiang) is a CIE color-appearance researcher; the paper builds a quantitative CIELAB-based harmony predictor from 1431 rated pairs.
caveats: Based on participants rating pairs (largely in UK and Taiwan); predicts average ratings only; model terms are approximate regression fits, not laws.

title: Color naming models for color selection, image editing and palette design
container: Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '12)
authority: Heer (University of Washington) and Stone (Tableau, StoneSoup Consulting) are leading visualization and color-for-display researchers.
caveats: Names come from the XKCD online survey (English-speaking, self-selected, uncalibrated monitors). Per-person and per-language differences are not modelled.

title: Vision and Art: The Biology of Seeing
authority: Livingstone is a Harvard neurobiologist who studied primate visual cortex; the book connects the luminance and color pathways to painting technique.
caveats: The strict 'Where vs What' separation is an oversimplification; the equiluminance effects on motion and depth are real but weaker than a clean dichotomy suggests.
